title: Why a Greek theatre lets you hear a whisper
description: Ancient Greek theatres were carved into hillsides in a perfect half-circle of stone seats — and their shape is so good that a whisper on stage can carry to the very back row.

body.heading: A hillside, hollowed
paragraphs: Greek builders chose a slope and carved the seating — the theatron, or 'seeing place' — directly into it, rising in concentric curved rows around a flat circular orchestra. Theatres like Epidaurus held well over ten thousand people, all facing the stage, all without a single speaker or microphone.

The curve does the work. Sound from the stage reflects off the orchestra floor and the stone seats in a way that carries voices upward and outward instead of letting them scatter, and the rising rows lift every listener clear of the heads — and the sound shadows — in front.

body.heading: Designed by ear
paragraphs: Later research found the seat rows themselves help: the regular corrugations of stone filter out low background rumble while passing the higher frequencies of speech, a stone-age sound engineer built into the furniture.
Actors also wore masks with mouth openings that may have helped project the voice. But the theatre itself was the amplifier — proof that careful shape can do what we now ask electronics to do.

takeaway: A Greek theatre is a stone amplifier: curved hillside seats, a reflecting floor and rows that filter rumble, carrying a stage whisper to the back row.
